examples.problem_statement: Solve the triangle ABC, given a = 30.3, b = 40.4, and c = 62.6. Refer to Fig. 31-15.

solution.result: a + b > c, a + c > b, b + c > a
solution.description: Before solving, confirm the three given lengths can actually close into a triangle: each pair must sum to more than the third, and 30.3 plus 40.4 is 70.7, which exceeds the longest side 62.6, so the triangle exists.

solution.operation: Calculate cos A using Law of Cosines
solution.description: All three sides are known and no angle is, so the Law of Cosines is the only entry point. Write it solved for cos A, with a, the side opposite A, in the subtracted position over twice the product of the two adjacent sides.
Substitute b = 40.4, c = 62.6 and a = 30.3: the squares give 1632.16 plus 3918.76 minus 918.09, which is 4632.83, over 2 times 40.4 times 62.6, which is 5058.08, so cos A is about 0.9159.
Take the inverse cosine of 0.9159 to get A near 23.67 degrees, then convert the decimal part to minutes, since 0.67 of a degree is about 40 minutes, giving A as 23 degrees 40 minutes.

solution.operation: Calculate cos B using Law of Cosines
solution.description: Repeat the same formula for the second angle, now isolating b, the side opposite B, so cos B uses a squared plus c squared minus b squared over 2ac.
Substitute a = 30.3, c = 62.6 and b = 40.4: 918.09 plus 3918.76 minus 1632.16 is 3204.69, and 2 times 30.3 times 62.6 is 3793.56, so cos B is about 0.8448.
Invert the cosine to get B near 32.33 degrees, and express the 0.33 of a degree as 20 minutes, giving B as 32 degrees 20 minutes.

solution.operation: Calculate angle C using angle sum property
solution.description: With two angles in hand the third follows from the angle sum: subtract 23 degrees 40 minutes and 32 degrees 20 minutes from 180 degrees, leaving C = 124 degrees 0 minutes. This is quicker than a third pass through the formula.

solution.operation: Verify using Law of Cosines for angle C
solution.description: As an independent check, compute cos C straight from the sides: 918.09 plus 1632.16 minus 3918.76 is -1368.51, over 2448.24, giving about -0.5589. The negative value already signals that C is obtuse.
The inverse cosine of -0.5589 is about 124.0 degrees, which matches the angle obtained from the 180 degree sum and confirms that all three angles are consistent.

common_mistakes: Pairing the wrong side with the angle: the side opposite the wanted angle is the one subtracted, so cos A uses b squared plus c squared minus a squared, not a squared plus b squared minus c squared.
Reading 23.67 degrees as 23 degrees 67 minutes; the decimal part must be multiplied by 60, which gives 40 minutes.
Dropping the minus sign on cos C of -0.5589, which would report the obtuse angle 124 degrees as 56 degrees.

concept.technique_name: Solving a trigonometric equation with the tangent addition formula

examples.problem_statement: A tower 150 m high is situated at the top of a hill. At a point 650 m down the hill the angle between the surface of the hill and the line of sight to the top of the tower is 12°30'. Find the inclination of the hill to a horizontal plane.

solution.description: Name the unknown and the data before any geometry: theta is the hill's inclination to the horizontal, the tower is 150 m high, the point of observation is 650 m down the slope, and the angle between the slope and the line of sight is 12 degrees 30 minutes, which is 12.5 degrees.

Fix the geometry in terms of theta: the slope rises at theta from the horizontal, so the line of sight to the tower top rises at theta plus 12.5 degrees, and the observation point lies 650 cos theta horizontally from the base of the tower's hill.

Express that line of sight angle as a tangent. The vertical rise to the tower top is the 150 m tower plus the 650 sin theta gained by walking up the slope, and the horizontal run is 650 cos theta, so their ratio is the tangent of theta plus 12.5 degrees.
Split the fraction into two pieces: the 650 sin theta over 650 cos theta part collapses to tan theta, leaving 150 over 650 cos theta plus tan theta on the right.
Expand the left side with the tangent addition formula so that the equation contains only tan theta and the known tangent of 12.5 degrees, ready for numerical substitution.

A hill inclination is small, so approximate cos theta by 1 and tan theta by theta measured in radians. This clears theta out of the denominator and turns a transcendental equation into an algebraic one.
Put in the numbers: tan 12.5 degrees is about 0.218 and 150 over 650 is 0.2308, leaving a single equation in theta with no trigonometric functions left.

Cross multiply to clear the denominator, expand the product on the right, and collect terms; the theta times theta term survives, giving the quadratic 0.218 theta squared minus 0.2191 theta plus 0.0128 equal to zero.
Apply the quadratic formula to that equation. Only the small positive root is physically meaningful for a hill, and it gives theta of about 0.096 radians, which converts to roughly 5.5 degrees.

examples.answer: The inclination of the hill is approximately 5.5°

solution.description: The problem supplies the linear function f of x equal to 3x minus 5, written as y = 3x - 5. It is one to one, so an inverse function exists, and finding that inverse is the goal.
An inverse sends outputs back to inputs, so interchange the roles of x and y to get x = 3y - 5. From this point on, solving for y produces the inverse rule.
Undo the subtraction first: add 5 to both sides of x = 3y - 5, which isolates the term containing y and gives x + 5 = 3y.
Undo the multiplication next: divide both sides by 3, so y equals the quantity x plus 5, all over 3.

Check the work by composing the two functions: 3 times the quantity x plus 5 over 3, minus 5, gives x plus 5 minus 5, which is x. The rule found really does undo f.

examples.problem_statement: Verify each of the following: (a) sin(Arcsin 1/2), (b) cos[Arccos(-1/2)], (c) cos[Arcsin(-sqrt(2)/2)], (d) Arcsin(sin pi/3), (e) Arccos[cos(-pi/4)], (f) Arcsin(tan 3pi/4), (g) Arccos[tan(-5pi/4)]

solution.description: State the property that drives parts (a) and (b): sine and arcsine undo each other, so the sine of arcsin x returns x itself, provided x lies between -1 and 1, where arcsine is defined.
Here the input is one half, which lies between -1 and 1, so the property applies with no further work and the value is one half.
State the matching property for the other pair: the cosine of arccos x returns x for any x between -1 and 1.
The input is negative one half, which lies in that interval, so the expression equals negative one half; the negative sign is no obstacle because arccosine accepts negative inputs.

Part (c) nests two different functions, so name the inner angle: let theta be the arcsine of negative root two over two, which means the sine of theta is negative root two over two. The task becomes finding the cosine of theta.

Get the cosine from the sine with the Pythagorean identity: 1 minus one half leaves one half for the square of the cosine. Because theta came out of arcsine it lies between negative pi over two and pi over two, where cosine is never negative.
Take the positive square root, which that range permits, so the cosine of theta is root two over two, and that is the value of the original nested expression.

In part (d) the inverse function is on the outside, so the principal range decides the answer: pi over 3 already lies between negative pi over two and pi over two, so arcsine hands back pi over 3 unchanged.

Part (e) has a negative input, but cosine is an even function, so the cosine of negative pi over 4 equals the cosine of pi over 4; since pi over 4 lies in the principal range from 0 to pi, arccosine returns pi over 4.
Part (f) must be worked from the inside out: evaluate the tangent of 3 pi over 4 first, which is -1, because that angle lies in the second quadrant where tangent is negative.
Now apply arcsine to the value just found: the arcsine of -1 is negative pi over two, the lower endpoint of the principal range.
Part (g) also starts on the inside: negative 5 pi over 4 is coterminal with 3 pi over 4 once 2 pi is added, and the tangent there is again -1.
Apply arccosine to that -1, which gives pi, the upper endpoint of the principal range from 0 to pi.

solution.description: Replace each inverse expression by the principal angle it names and then check the claimed identity by arithmetic on those angles: arcsin of root two over two is pi over 4 and arcsin of one half is pi over 6, whose difference is pi over 12; arccos 0 is pi over two and arctan of -1 is negative pi over 4, whose sum is pi over 4, which is arctan 1. Both statements verify.

examples.problem_statement: Evaluate each of the following: (a) cos(Arcsin 3/5), (b) sin[Arccos(-2/3)], (c) tan[Arcsin(-3/4)]

solution.description: Give the inner inverse expression a name: let theta be the angle it returns, and note which quadrant its principal range places theta in, since that quadrant fixes the signs of the remaining ratios.
Build a reference right triangle for theta from the given ratio, using the Pythagorean theorem to supply the missing side, for example legs 3 and 4 with hypotenuse 5 for the angle whose sine is 3/5.

Read the outer function off that triangle as a ratio of its sides and attach the sign the quadrant of theta requires, which yields 4/5 for part (a), root 5 over 3 for part (b) and negative 3 root 7 over 7 for part (c).
Name the two angles being added: one has sine 12/13 and the other has sine 4/5, and both lie in the principal range of arcsine, so both are first quadrant angles.
Expand the sine of the sum with the addition formula, which needs the cosine of each angle as well as its sine; the Pythagorean identity supplies 5/13 and 3/5, both positive in the first quadrant.
Substitute the four ratios into the expanded formula: 12/13 times 3/5 plus 5/13 times 4/5 gives 36/65 plus 20/65, which is 56/65.

solution.description: Both terms contain sin x, so factor it out instead of dividing by it, which turns the equation into the product of sin x and the quantity 1 minus 2 cos x, set equal to zero.
A product is zero only when one of its factors is zero, so split the single equation into two simpler ones: sin x = 0, and 1 minus 2 cos x = 0.
Sine vanishes at every integer multiple of pi, so x = n pi for integer n; restricted to the interval from 0 up to 2 pi this contributes x = 0 and x = pi.

solution.description: Separate each number into its two components before combining anything: the first has real part 2 and imaginary part 3, the second has real part 4 and imaginary part negative 5. The minus sign belongs to the 5.
Real parts add exactly like ordinary numbers, so 2 plus 4 gives 6.
Imaginary parts add the same way with i kept as a common factor: 3i plus negative 5i is 3 minus 5, all times i, which is negative 2i.
Reassemble the two sums into standard form with the real part written first, so 6 plus negative 2i is written 6 minus 2i.
Check the result geometrically: the two numbers are the points (2, 3) and (4, -5) in the complex plane, and adding them as vectors lands on (6, -2), which is the same number 6 minus 2i.
Subtraction works component by component just as addition does, so take the real parts in the given order: 2 minus 4 is negative 2.
Subtract the imaginary parts, watching the sign of the second number: 3 minus negative 5 becomes 3 plus 5, which is 8, so the imaginary part grows instead of shrinking.
Write the two components back together in standard form, real part first, as negative 2 plus 8i.
Multiplication is not done component by component; treat the two numbers as binomials and distribute all four products, giving 8, negative 10i, 12i and negative 15 times i squared.
Combine the two like imaginary terms, negative 10i and 12i, into 2i, leaving 8 plus 2i minus 15 times i squared.
Use the defining property that i squared is negative 1, so negative 15 times i squared becomes plus 15.
Add the two real pieces, 8 and 15, to reach the standard form 23 plus 2i.

common_mistakes: Multiplying component by component, as 2 times 4 plus 3i times negative 5i, instead of expanding all four binomial products.
Losing a sign when subtracting: 3 minus negative 5 is 8, not negative 2.
Replacing i squared by 1 instead of negative 1, or leaving i squared in the answer, which turns 23 plus 2i into negative 7 plus 2i.
